Aerial view of the White House in Washington, D.C., in the summer of 1955, filmed from a low-flying aircraft high above Lafayette Square, looking south. In the foreground, Pennsylvania Avenue with a few rounded 1950s cars, and beyond its iron fence the wide, deep North Lawn with its round fountain and a semicircular asphalt driveway curving from two gates on Pennsylvania Avenue up to the columned North Portico and back. The white mansion stands well back from the street and is by far the largest and tallest building in view. On either side of it, much smaller, single-storey white wings sit low and half hidden among the trees: the West Wing on the right and the East Wing on the left, each joined to the house by a low colonnade. Beyond the house, open green parkland: the South Lawn, then the large green oval of the Ellipse, and behind it the Washington Monument rising alone from open grounds, no buildings in between. Warm late-afternoon sun, long soft shadows. Wide aerial shot looking down at an angle.

On the left, an engineer seen from behind, in a white shirt with rolled-up sleeves, his raised hand pinning a clipping from a Soviet newspaper to the board; the clipping's headline "США ЗАПУСТЯТ ИСКУССТВЕННЫЙ СПУТНИК ЗЕМЛИ" in bold Russian newspaper type. In the corner beside the board, a large red Soviet flag with the golden hammer and sickle and the gold-bordered star in its upper corner hangs from a flagpole. Above the board, a red propaganda poster with a big golden hammer and sickle. A heavy wooden desk in the foreground with an unlit metal desk lamp, a glass of tea in a metal holder and a slide rule. Cold blue moonlight from a tall window, the room dim. Medium shot, 50mm lens.

A small polished metal sphere, about half a metre across, with four long thin straight antennas sweeping back from it in a narrow V, in orbit high above the Earth. The sphere's mirror-bright surface catches the sun and reflects the planet below. Beneath it the curved Earth at the edge of night: on one side oceans and clouds in daylight, on the other the darkened hemisphere. The sphere sits in the left third of the frame, seen slightly from below and behind.

Photorealistic, as if filmed by a camera in Earth orbit: pure black space, hard unfiltered sunlight with deep shadows, the thin glowing blue line of the atmosphere along the Earth's limb, clouds and oceans in fine detail, no stars visible. Cinematic, sharp, a still frame from a feature film.

Close-up of a 1950s news-agency teleprinter in a Moscow office, 1955: a bulky dark grey machine on a metal stand, its rounded sheet-metal hood with a small glass window over the printing mechanism, a wide continuous roll of pale yellow paper rising out of a slot in the top of the hood and curling over the back. The printed line "U.S. TO LAUNCH EARTH SATELLITE" in typewriter capitals is clearly legible on the paper just above the slot. Behind it, more teleprinters in a row along the wall of a news room. Hard window light from the left, dust in the air, a cold glass of tea in a metal holder on a shelf beside the machine. 85mm lens, shallow depth of field, the paper in sharp focus.
